title: Permissions and Ownership
subtitle: chmod, chown, rwx bits, sudo — understanding who can do what with files
author: KERNAL Team

content.code:
ls -l deploy.sh
-rwxr-xr-x  1  alice  developers  4096  Oct 6  deploy.sh

Permissions: -rwxr-xr-x
  Position 1:     - = regular file, d = directory, l = symlink
  Positions 2-4:  rwx = owner permissions
  Positions 5-7:  r-x = group permissions
  Positions 8-10: r-x = others permissions

  r = read    (value: 4)
  w = write   (value: 2)
  x = execute (value: 1)
  - = no permission (value: 0)

Octal (numeric) notation:
  rwx = 4+2+1 = 7
  r-x = 4+0+1 = 5
  r-- = 4+0+0 = 4
  --- = 0+0+0 = 0

Common permission sets:
  755 = rwxr-xr-x  (executable: owner full, others read+execute)
  644 = rw-r--r--  (file: owner read+write, others read only)
  600 = rw-------  (private file: owner only — use for SSH keys)
  700 = rwx------  (private directory: owner only)

# Numeric (octal) mode
chmod 755 deploy.sh      # rwxr-xr-x
chmod 644 config.txt     # rw-r--r--
chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_rsa  # rw------- (SSH private key must be 600)
chmod -R 755 /var/www/   # -R: apply recursively to directory

# Symbolic mode
chmod +x deploy.sh       # add execute for everyone
chmod -w notes.txt       # remove write for everyone
chmod u+x,g-w script.sh  # user add execute, group remove write
chmod o-rwx secret.txt   # remove all permissions for others

# Make a script executable (most common use)
chmod +x myscript.sh
./myscript.sh

# sudo: run a command as the superuser (root)
sudo apt install nginx       # install with admin rights
sudo systemctl start nginx   # start a service
sudo nano /etc/hosts         # edit a system file

# Become root (use sparingly)
sudo -i

# chown: change ownership
sudo chown alice file.txt           # change owner to alice
sudo chown alice:developers dir/    # owner:group
sudo chown -R alice:alice /home/alice/  # recursive

content.text: SSH keys must be 600. If your SSH private key has permissions looser than 600 (rw-------), SSH will refuse to use it with 'Permissions too open'. Fix: chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_rsa

questions.question: What permissions does chmod 644 set?
options: rwxr-xr-x — owner full access, others read+execute
rw-r--r-- — owner read+write, group and others read-only
rwx------ — owner full, others no access
questions.explanation: 644 in octal: 6 = rw- (4+2+0), 4 = r-- (4+0+0), 4 = r-- (4+0+0). So: rw-r--r-- — the owner can read and write, everyone else can only read. This is the standard permission for regular files like config files, text files, and source code.

faq.a: When modifying system files (/etc, /var, /usr), installing packages, managing services (systemctl), or changing ownership of files not owned by you. On your own home directory and files, you do not need sudo. The rule: try without sudo first. If you get 'Permission denied', then consider if sudo is appropriate — don't sudo everything reflexively.

examples: chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_rsa is required before SSH will use a private key — a daily developer task
Web servers need chmod 755 on directories and 644 on files for Nginx/Apache to serve them correctly
